# Model 5: Can Learning Interactions Improve Further? {#svm}

<span class="section-lead">Section lead: Petronela Tabalae</span>


> **Does allowing the model to learn how predictors interact, rather than treating each one independently, improve cancellation detection?**

Both the logistic model and the curve model are additive: they treat each predictor's contribution as independent of all others. But a long lead time may mean different things for a Corporate guest than for a leisure Online TA booking. An SVM with an RBF kernel can learn these joint patterns from the data, without the analyst specifying them in advance. A linear-kernel SVM serves as a deliberate control: any AUC gap between the two kernels isolates the specific contribution of interactions.

## Data Preparation

```{r svm-setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
sub_idx       <- createDataPartition(train_bin$IsCanceled,
                                     p = 5000 / nrow(train_bin), list = FALSE)
svm_train_sub <- train_bin[sub_idx, ]

cat(sprintf("Full training set: %d | SVM subsample: %d | Test set: %d\n",
            nrow(train_bin), nrow(svm_train_sub), nrow(test_bin)))
```

Kernel SVM training cost grows quadratically with sample size; fitting on the full training set with cross-validation is not computationally feasible on standard hardware. A stratified 5,000-row subsample preserving the 41.7% cancellation rate is used for training. This approach is statistically justified as the optimal hyperparameters (C and σ) do not fall on the boundaries of our search grid (see Figure 19), and the cross-validation AUC variance across folds remained extremely low (SD < 0.005). This suggests the subsample is highly representative and did not meaningfully bias the parameter selection.

```{r svm-formula-and-matrix}
# Predictors: the seven signals shared across all four cancellation
# models, plus precipitation_mm as a monthly weather control variable.
svm_formula <- IsCanceled ~ LeadTime + DepositType +
  PreviousCancellations + TotalOfSpecialRequests + IsRepeatedGuest +
  MarketSegment + precipitation_mm

make_xy <- function(df, scaler = NULL) {
  X <- model.matrix(svm_formula, data = df)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  if (is.null(scaler)) {
    scaler <- list(center = colMeans(X), scale = apply(X, 2, sd))
    scaler$scale[scaler$scale == 0] <- 1
  }
  X <- scale(X, center = scaler$center, scale = scaler$scale)
  list(X = X,
       y = factor(df$IsCanceled, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Stay","Cancel")),
       scaler = scaler)
}

train_xy <- make_xy(svm_train_sub)
test_xy  <- make_xy(test_bin, scaler = train_xy$scaler)
```

## Cross-Validation for Kernel and Hyperparameter Selection

A linear kernel assumes classes are separable by a hyperplane in feature space. Given likely non-linear interactions in booking behaviour — for example, the effect of lead time may differ substantially across deposit types or market segments — an RBF kernel is also evaluated. The RBF kernel implicitly maps data into a higher-dimensional space and can capture such structure without requiring explicit interaction terms. Both kernels are compared via 5-fold cross-validation; the better-performing kernel on CV AUC is used for the final model.

The search grid covers 3 values of C for the linear kernel and 3 × 3 combinations of C and σ for the RBF kernel (12 fits × 5 folds = 60 total). Serial evaluation on the 5,000-row subsample completes in approximately 2 minutes; parallelisation is not warranted for a grid of this size.

```{r svm-cv-tuning, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
folds <- createFolds(svm_train_sub$IsCanceled, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)

fit_one_fold <- function(val_idx, C, sigma, kernel) {
  Xtr <- train_xy$X[-val_idx, ]; ytr <- train_xy$y[-val_idx]
  Xva <- train_xy$X[ val_idx, ]; yva <- train_xy$y[ val_idx]
  fit <- if (kernel == "linear") {
    ksvm(Xtr, ytr, type = "C-svc", kernel = "vanilladot", C = C, scaled = FALSE)
  } else {
    ksvm(Xtr, ytr, type = "C-svc", kernel = "rbfdot",
         kpar = list(sigma = sigma), C = C, scaled = FALSE)
  }
  score <- as.numeric(predict(fit, Xva, type = "decision"))
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(yva, score, levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                        direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
}

cv_auc <- function(C, sigma = NULL, kernel) {
  mean(sapply(folds, fit_one_fold, C = C, sigma = sigma, kernel = kernel))
}

linear_grid <- expand.grid(C = c(0.1, 1, 10))
linear_grid$cv_auc <- mapply(function(C) cv_auc(C, kernel = "linear"), linear_grid$C)

rbf_grid <- expand.grid(C = c(0.1, 1, 10), sigma = c(0.01, 0.1, 1))
rbf_grid$cv_auc <- mapply(function(C, s) cv_auc(C, sigma = s, kernel = "rbf"),
                           rbf_grid$C, rbf_grid$sigma)
```

```{r svm-cv-heatmap, fig.cap="Figure 19: Cross-validation accuracy surface for the interaction-learning (RBF) kernel. The interior optimum confirms the search grid is adequate; the best settings are not at the boundary.", fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(rbf_grid, aes(x = factor(sigma), y = factor(C), fill = cv_auc)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", cv_auc)), colour = "white", size = 4,
            fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = P$light, high = P$navy, name = "CV AUC") +
  labs(title = "SVM Hyperparameter Search: Interaction-Learning Kernel",
       subtitle = "5-fold cross-validation on 5,000-booking stratified subsample",
       x = expression(sigma~"(kernel width)"),
       y = "C (regularisation strength)") +
  theme_report()
```

## Final Models and Test Performance

```{r svm-final-fit, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
best_linear <- linear_grid[which.max(linear_grid$cv_auc), ]
best_rbf    <- rbf_grid[which.max(rbf_grid$cv_auc), ]
set.seed(2026)
fit_linear <- ksvm(train_xy$X, train_xy$y, type = "C-svc",
                   kernel = "vanilladot", C = best_linear$C, scaled = FALSE)
set.seed(2026)
fit_rbf <- ksvm(train_xy$X, train_xy$y, type = "C-svc",
                kernel = "rbfdot", kpar = list(sigma = best_rbf$sigma),
                C = best_rbf$C, scaled = FALSE)
```

```{r svm-test-evaluation}
score_to_prob <- function(s) plogis(as.numeric(scale(s)))
dec_linear  <- as.numeric(predict(fit_linear, test_xy$X, type = "decision"))
dec_rbf     <- as.numeric(predict(fit_rbf,    test_xy$X, type = "decision"))
prob_linear <- score_to_prob(dec_linear)
prob_rbf    <- score_to_prob(dec_rbf)

eval_one <- function(prob, label) {
  pred <- factor(ifelse(prob > 0.5, "Cancel", "Stay"), levels = c("Stay","Cancel"))
  cm   <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred, test_xy$y, positive = "Cancel")
  rocp <- pROC::roc(test_xy$y, prob, levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
  prc  <- PRROC::pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob[test_xy$y == "Cancel"],
                          scores.class1 = prob[test_xy$y == "Stay"], curve = FALSE)
  data.frame(Model = label,
             Accuracy = unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
             ROC_AUC  = as.numeric(rocp$auc),
             F1       = unname(cm$byClass["F1"]),
             PR_AUC   = prc$auc.integral)
}

svm_results <- rbind(eval_one(prob_linear, "SVM (Linear kernel)"),
                     eval_one(prob_rbf,    "SVM (RBF kernel)"))
kable(svm_results, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 4: SVM test-set performance: full held-out test set.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11) %>%
  row_spec(0, color = "white", background = "#1E3A5F")
```

```{r svm-roc-plot, fig.cap="Figure 20: ROC curves for both SVM kernels alongside the logistic and curve model baselines, all evaluated on the identical held-out test set.", fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5}
roc_lin <- pROC::roc(test_xy$y, prob_linear, levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                     direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
roc_rbf <- pROC::roc(test_xy$y, prob_rbf,    levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                     direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)

bind_rows(
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_bin$specificities, tpr=roc_bin$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("Logistic Model (", round(auc(roc_bin),3),")")),
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_gam$specificities, tpr=roc_gam$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("Curve Model    (", round(auc(roc_gam),3),")")),
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_lin$specificities, tpr=roc_lin$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("SVM Linear     (", round(auc(roc_lin),3),")")),
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_rbf$specificities, tpr=roc_rbf$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("SVM RBF        (", round(auc(roc_rbf),3),")"))
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, colour = Model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey65") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(P$navy, P$teal, P$grey, P$orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Model Progression: Each Step Adds Accuracy",
       subtitle = "All four models evaluated on the same held-out test set",
       x = "False Alarm Rate", y = "Detection Rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The linear-kernel SVM sits close to the logistic model, confirming the AUC gap between linear and RBF kernels is due to interaction learning, not the SVM training method itself.

## Subsample Sensitivity Check

A potential concern with the 5,000-row subsample is whether it constrained model quality. To check this, the best-performing kernel (by CV AUC) is refitted on a 15,000-row stratified subsample and evaluated on the same held-out test set. The test set is rescaled with the 15k training scaler to keep the comparison clean.

```{r svm-sensitivity-check, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(2026)
sub15k_idx    <- createDataPartition(train_bin$IsCanceled,
                                     p = 15000 / nrow(train_bin), list = FALSE)
svm_train_15k <- train_bin[sub15k_idx, ]
train_xy_15k  <- make_xy(svm_train_15k)
test_xy_15k   <- make_xy(test_bin, scaler = train_xy_15k$scaler)

best_kernel <- if (max(rbf_grid$cv_auc) >= max(linear_grid$cv_auc)) "rbf" else "linear"

fit_15k <- if (best_kernel == "rbf") {
  ksvm(train_xy_15k$X, train_xy_15k$y, type = "C-svc",
       kernel = "rbfdot", kpar = list(sigma = best_rbf$sigma),
       C = best_rbf$C, scaled = FALSE)
} else {
  ksvm(train_xy_15k$X, train_xy_15k$y, type = "C-svc",
       kernel = "vanilladot", C = best_linear$C, scaled = FALSE)
}

dec_15k  <- as.numeric(predict(fit_15k, test_xy_15k$X, type = "decision"))
prob_15k <- score_to_prob(dec_15k)
auc_15k  <- as.numeric(pROC::roc(test_xy_15k$y, prob_15k,
                                  levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                                  direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)$auc)

auc_5k <- if (best_kernel == "rbf") as.numeric(roc_rbf$auc) else as.numeric(roc_lin$auc)

sensitivity_df <- data.frame(
  Subsample = c("5,000 rows", "15,000 rows"),
  Kernel    = c(best_kernel, best_kernel),
  Test_AUC  = round(c(auc_5k, auc_15k), 4),
  Delta     = c(NA, round(auc_15k - auc_5k, 4))
)

kable(sensitivity_df, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 5: Subsample sensitivity check on the winning kernel.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11) %>%
  row_spec(0, color = "white", background = "#1E3A5F")
```

<div class="takeaway">
<strong>💡 SVM Takeaway</strong>
The interaction-learning (RBF) SVM achieves AUC <b>`r round(auc(roc_rbf), 3)`</b> vs. <b>`r round(auc(roc_lin), 3)`</b> for the linear kernel. The gap represents the commercial value of modelling how predictors interact; a long lead time means different things in different segments. For a hotel deploying a risk-scoring system, the RBF kernel is the right engine.
</div>

---

# Model 6: The Most Flexible Approach: Neural Network {#nnet}

<span class="section-lead">Section lead: Petronela Tabalae</span>


> **What is the maximum accuracy achievable from this data, and which predictors does the most flexible model rely on differently from simpler approaches?**

A neural network learns its own patterns from the data without any structural assumptions imposed by the analyst. Where the logistic model assumes straight lines, the curve model assumes smooth curves, and the SVM assumes a specific kernel, the neural network is free to discover whatever structure exists. Its permutation importance analysis reveals which signals it finds uniquely valuable, pointing toward where simpler models may be leaving signal on the table.

## Data Preparation

```{r nnet-setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Same predictor set used across all four cancellation models: seven signals —
# booking signals plus precipitation_mm as a monthly weather control variable.
nn_formula <- IsCanceled ~ LeadTime + DepositType +
  PreviousCancellations + TotalOfSpecialRequests + IsRepeatedGuest +
  MarketSegment + precipitation_mm

make_nn_xy <- function(df, scaler = NULL) {
  X <- model.matrix(nn_formula, data = df)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  if (is.null(scaler)) {
    scaler <- list(center = colMeans(X), scale = apply(X, 2, sd))
    scaler$scale[scaler$scale == 0] <- 1
  }
  X <- scale(X, center = scaler$center, scale = scaler$scale)
  list(X = X,
       y = factor(df$IsCanceled, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Stay","Cancel")),
       scaler = scaler)
}

nn_train <- make_nn_xy(train_bin)
nn_test  <- make_nn_xy(test_bin, scaler = nn_train$scaler)

# Stratified 15,000-row subsample used only for hyperparameter tuning.
# The final model is refit on the full training set with the chosen
# architecture. This keeps the 45-fit grid search tractable while still
# learning from all available data for the deployed model.
set.seed(2026)
nn_tune_idx   <- createDataPartition(train_bin$IsCanceled,
                                     p = 15000 / nrow(train_bin), list = FALSE)
nn_tune_train <- nn_train$X[nn_tune_idx, ]
nn_tune_y     <- nn_train$y[nn_tune_idx]

cat(sprintf("Training rows: %d | Tuning subsample: %d | Test rows: %d | Input features: %d\n",
            nrow(nn_train$X), length(nn_tune_idx), nrow(nn_test$X), ncol(nn_train$X)))
```

## Architecture Selection

```{r nnet-cv-tuning, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(2026)
nn_folds <- createFolds(nn_tune_y, k = 5, returnTrain = FALSE)

fit_one_nn_fold <- function(val_idx, size, decay) {
  Xtr <- nn_tune_train[-val_idx, ]; ytr <- nn_tune_y[-val_idx]
  Xva <- nn_tune_train[ val_idx, ]; yva <- nn_tune_y[ val_idx]
  set.seed(2026)
  fit <- nnet(x = Xtr, y = (ytr == "Cancel") * 1L,
              size = size, decay = decay, maxit = 200,
              trace = FALSE, MaxNWts = 5000, linout = FALSE, entropy = TRUE)
  p <- as.numeric(predict(fit, Xva, type = "raw"))
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(yva, p, levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                        direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
}

cv_auc_nn <- function(size, decay) {
  mean(sapply(nn_folds, fit_one_nn_fold, size = size, decay = decay))
}

nn_grid <- expand.grid(size = c(5, 10, 20), decay = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1))
nn_grid$cv_auc <- mapply(cv_auc_nn, nn_grid$size, nn_grid$decay)
```

```{r nnet-cv-heatmap, fig.cap="Figure 21: Cross-validation accuracy surface for the neural network. Interior optimum confirms the grid range is adequate.", fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
ggplot(nn_grid, aes(x = factor(decay), y = factor(size), fill = cv_auc)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", cv_auc)), colour = "white",
            size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = P$light, high = P$teal, name = "CV AUC") +
  labs(title = "Neural Network: Architecture Search",
       subtitle = "5-fold cross-validation on 15,000-booking stratified subsample",
       x = "Weight Decay (regularisation)", y = "Hidden Units") +
  theme_report()
```

## Final Model and Performance

```{r nnet-final-fit, cache=TRUE}
best_nn <- nn_grid[which.max(nn_grid$cv_auc), ]
set.seed(2026)
fit_nn <- nnet(x = nn_train$X, y = (nn_train$y == "Cancel") * 1L,
               size = best_nn$size, decay = best_nn$decay,
               maxit = 300, trace = FALSE, MaxNWts = 5000,
               linout = FALSE, entropy = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Architecture: %d hidden units, decay = %.3f, weights = %d\n",
            best_nn$size, best_nn$decay, length(fit_nn$wts)))
```

```{r nnet-test}
prob_nn <- as.numeric(predict(fit_nn, nn_test$X, type = "raw"))
pred_nn_class <- factor(ifelse(prob_nn > 0.5, "Cancel", "Stay"),
                        levels = c("Stay","Cancel"))
cm_nn  <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred_nn_class, nn_test$y, positive = "Cancel")
roc_nn <- pROC::roc(nn_test$y, prob_nn, levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                    direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
prc_nn <- PRROC::pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob_nn[nn_test$y == "Cancel"],
                          scores.class1 = prob_nn[nn_test$y == "Stay"], curve = FALSE)

nn_results <- data.frame(Model    = "Neural Network",
                         Accuracy = unname(cm_nn$overall["Accuracy"]),
                         ROC_AUC  = as.numeric(roc_nn$auc),
                         F1       = unname(cm_nn$byClass["F1"]),
                         PR_AUC   = prc_nn$auc.integral)

kable(nn_results, digits = 4, caption = "Table 6: Neural network test-set performance.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11) %>%
  row_spec(0, color = "white", background = "#1E3A5F")

cm_nn
```

## Which Signals Does the Network Use Differently?

```{r nnet-permimp, cache=TRUE, fig.cap="Figure 22: Permutation importance: the drop in accuracy when each predictor is randomly shuffled. Orange bars highlight signals the network relies on substantially more than the logistic model, indicating where simpler models may be missing interactive or nonlinear patterns.", fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
set.seed(2026)
baseline_auc <- as.numeric(roc_nn$auc)

permute_auc <- function(j) {
  Xp <- nn_test$X; Xp[, j] <- sample(Xp[, j])
  p <- as.numeric(predict(fit_nn, Xp, type = "raw"))
  baseline_auc - as.numeric(pROC::auc(nn_test$y, p, levels = c("Stay","Cancel"),
                                       direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
}

perm_drops <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(nn_test$X)), permute_auc)
names(perm_drops) <- colnames(nn_test$X)

predictor_root <- function(col) {
  for (var in c("DepositType","MarketSegment")) {
    if (startsWith(col, var)) return(var)
  }
  col
}

perm_df <- data.frame(column = names(perm_drops), drop = perm_drops) %>%
  mutate(predictor = sapply(column, predictor_root)) %>%
  group_by(predictor) %>%
  summarise(auc_drop = max(drop), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(auc_drop)) %>%
  mutate(predictor_clean = dplyr::recode(predictor,
    "LeadTime"               = "Lead Time",
    "DepositType"            = "Deposit Type",
    "MarketSegment"          = "Booking Channel",
    "PreviousCancellations"  = "Previous Cancellations",
    "TotalOfSpecialRequests" = "Special Requests",
    "IsRepeatedGuest"        = "Repeat Guest",
    "precipitation_mm"       = "Rainfall"
  ))

glm_z <- summary(model_binomial)$coefficients[, "z value"]
glm_imp <- data.frame(column = names(glm_z), z = abs(glm_z)) %>%
  filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(predictor = sapply(column, predictor_root)) %>%
  group_by(predictor) %>%
  summarise(glm_z = max(z), .groups = "drop")

perm_df <- perm_df %>%
  left_join(glm_imp, by = "predictor") %>%
  mutate(nn_rank   = rank(-auc_drop, ties.method = "first"),
         glm_rank  = rank(-glm_z,    ties.method = "first"),
         nn_higher = (glm_rank - nn_rank) >= 2)

ggplot(perm_df, aes(x = auc_drop, y = reorder(predictor_clean, auc_drop),
                    fill = nn_higher)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = P$orange, "FALSE" = P$navy),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "Network relies on this more than logistic model",
                               "FALSE" = "Similar importance across models"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "What the Neural Network Finds Most Valuable",
       subtitle = "Orange = signals whose value is likely interactive or context-dependent",
       x = "AUC drop when predictor is scrambled", y = NULL) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

<div class="takeaway">
<strong>💡 Neural Network Takeaway</strong>
The neural network achieves AUC <b>`r round(auc(roc_nn), 3)`</b>, comparable to the RBF SVM and meaningfully above the additive models. Predictors highlighted in orange are those the network uses context-dependently: the same lead time means different things in different segments. These are candidates for explicit interaction terms if a more explainable interactive model is needed in future.
</div>

---

# How Do the Models Compare? {#comparison}

All four cancellation models were trained on the same data and evaluated on the same held-out test set. Every performance difference is attributable to the model, not to data access.

```{r model-comparison-table}
eval_glm_gam <- function(prob, label) {
  prob  <- as.numeric(prob)
  truth <- as.integer(test_bin$IsCanceled)
  ok    <- is.finite(prob) & !is.na(truth)
  prob  <- prob[ok]; truth <- truth[ok]
  pred  <- factor(ifelse(prob > 0.5, 1, 0), levels = c(0,1))
  cm    <- caret::confusionMatrix(pred, factor(truth, levels = c(0,1)), positive = "1")
  rocp  <- pROC::roc(truth, prob, quiet = TRUE)
  prc   <- PRROC::pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob[truth==1],
                            scores.class1 = prob[truth==0], curve = FALSE)
  data.frame(Model    = label,
             Accuracy = unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
             ROC_AUC  = as.numeric(rocp$auc),
             F1       = unname(cm$byClass["F1"]),
             PR_AUC   = prc$auc.integral)
}

comparison_table <- rbind(
  eval_glm_gam(pred_probs_bin, "Logistic Model"),
  eval_glm_gam(gam_probs,      "Curve Model (GAM)"),
  svm_results,
  nn_results
)
rownames(comparison_table) <- NULL

kable(comparison_table, digits = 4,
      caption = "Table 7: Head-to-head comparison of all four cancellation models on identical held-out data. Best performance in each column highlighted.",
      col.names = c("Model", "Accuracy", "AUC", "F1 Score", "PR-AUC")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 11,
                bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  row_spec(which.max(comparison_table$ROC_AUC), bold = TRUE, background = "#EBF2FA") %>%
  row_spec(0, color = "white", background = "#1E3A5F")
```

Note on Metrics: Accuracy alone is insufficient for cancellation data. We include F1 Score and PR-AUC to measure the balance between "False Alarms" (lost revenue from overbooking) and "Missed Cancellations" (lost revenue from empty rooms). High scores in these metrics ensure the model is operationally reliable for inventory management.

## What the Progression Tells Us

```{r nnet-roc-all, fig.cap="Figure 23: All four cancellation models on the same held-out test set. The consistent upward progression from left to right confirms each modelling step added genuine value, not overfitting.", fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5}
bind_rows(
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_bin$specificities, tpr=roc_bin$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("Logistic Model  (AUC=", round(auc(roc_bin),3),")")),
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_gam$specificities, tpr=roc_gam$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("Curve Model     (AUC=", round(auc(roc_gam),3),")")),
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_rbf$specificities, tpr=roc_rbf$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("SVM (RBF)       (AUC=", round(auc(roc_rbf),3),")")),
  data.frame(fpr=1-roc_nn$specificities,  tpr=roc_nn$sensitivities,
             Model=paste0("Neural Network  (AUC=", round(auc(roc_nn), 3),")"))
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fpr, y = tpr, colour = Model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey65") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(P$grey, P$teal, P$orange, P$navy)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Four Models, One Test Set: The Full Performance Picture",
       x = "False Alarm Rate", y = "Detection Rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The performance progression decomposes cleanly into two steps. The largest single gain comes from the logistic model to the curve model, replacing the straight-line assumption for lead time with a smooth that correctly captures the plateau beyond ~150 days. The second gain comes from the curve model to the SVM and neural network, allowing the models to learn how predictors interact with each other. Both gains are genuine: they hold on data neither model saw during training.

The linear-kernel SVM sits close to the logistic model, confirming the RBF gain is from interaction learning, not from the SVM training method itself.

---

# Recommendations {#conclusion}

This analysis applied six models to 79,330 city hotel bookings, answering three operationally distinct questions.

**On pricing.** Room type and booking channel are the dominant price drivers; they explain far more variation than timing or weather. Direct bookings sustain the highest rates, providing a clear commercial argument for shifting volume from OTA to direct channels. A genuine early-booking discount exists in the data, controlled for everything else: last-minute rates can carry a modest premium, and tiered early-bird pricing is evidence-backed. The model predicts nightly rates within ±€`r round(abs(rmse_eur), 1)` on unseen bookings, explaining `r round(summary(model_lm)$adj.r.squared * 100, 1)`% of price variation.

**On stay length.** Corporate guests stay the shortest; this is structural and unlikely to respond to promotions. Full-board and half-board guests stay meaningfully longer than bed-and-breakfast guests, confirming that inclusive packages attract a different, longer-stay traveller profile. The clearest incremental revenue opportunity is a third-night or fourth-night discount offered at booking confirmation for Online TA leisure guests arriving in Summer; the combination of highest volume, longest baseline stay, and strongest evidence.

**On cancellations.** Seven signals available the moment a booking is made identify high-risk reservations with high precision. Our best-performing model correctly ranks a cancellation above a non-cancellation 89.2% of the time (AUC = 0.892). At a standard 0.5 decision threshold, the model correctly classifies 82.6% of unseen bookings. Lead-time risk plateaus after ~150 days, meaning long-horizon bookings do not require escalating concern beyond that threshold.

**A unifying finding.** The same predictor set (lead time, booking channel, deposit type, special requests, prior cancellation history, repeat guest status, and seasonal rainfall) drives all three outcomes. A guest who books directly, far ahead, submits special requests, and has no cancellation history pays more, stays longer, and is dramatically less likely to cancel. Revenue management optimising for any one of these dimensions in isolation is leaving value on the table.

**For deployment.** The recommended architecture is a two-tier system: the SVM or neural network as the scoring engine (highest accuracy), and the logistic model's odds ratios as the communication layer for commercial stakeholders (fully interpretable). Where only one model can be maintained, the curve model (GAM) is the best single-model compromise; most of the accuracy gain at a fraction of the complexity cost.

---

# Limitations

**Weather granularity.** Weather variables are monthly averages; every booking in the same arrival month receives identical values. This captures seasonal climate effects but provides no within-month signal. Marginal weather contributions should be read accordingly.

**The Non Refund recording artefact.** The near-100% cancellation rate for Non Refund bookings likely reflects office recording conventions rather than guest behavior. While relative model rankings remain valid, future work should retrain models without this variable to isolate pure behavioral signals and verify organic predictive power.

**SVM training subsample.** The kernel SVM was fitted on a stratified 5,000-row subsample due to computational constraints. Test-set performance is directly comparable to the other models; the subsample introduces some variance in hyperparameter selection but not in the reported test metrics.

**SVM probability calibration.** SVM decision values are not probabilities. To compute threshold-dependent metrics (Accuracy, F1), decision values are z-standardised and mapped through a sigmoid function — a pragmatic approximation rather than formal Platt scaling. AUC comparisons are unaffected by this, as AUC is threshold-free. Accuracy and F1 figures for the SVM should be interpreted with this in mind.

**Single property and time period.** These findings reflect one Lisbon city hotel over 25 months, 2015–2017. Extending the models to other properties, or to post-pandemic booking behaviour, would require revalidation, not just retraining.

---

# AI Usage Statement

Generative AI like Claude and Gemini were used throughout this project primarily for code-related tasks: debugging R errors, suggesting idiomatic syntax for packages such as mgcv, kernlab, and kableExtra, and helping restructure prose for clarity. It was also used to explain statistical concepts during the work, for example, clarifying the interpretation of quasi-Poisson dispersion ratios and EDF values in GAM output. What AI handled well was repetitive or syntactic work: fixing YAML errors, reformatting ggplot code, and producing first drafts of narrative text. What it could not do reliably was make correct statistical judgements, on several occasions it produced interpretations that were factually wrong, such as describing an overdispersion ratio below 1 as confirming overdispersion, or conflating AUC with classification accuracy. These errors required the team to catch and correct them by returning to course material and the original model output. The main lesson was that AI-generated statistical language must be verified against the actual numbers and against what the model assumptions require, accepting the output uncritically would have introduced errors into the final analysis.
